title: Our Solar System
logline: On a clear night a girl asks about a bright 'star', and her questions carry her and her Gran on an imagined journey from the Sun out past Pluto, until home is a single blue dot, and then back to their hill as the Sun comes up.
note: One continuous family film of about 15 minutes, grown out of the Saturn chapter (films/saturn). Built by six part teams in films/sf-a … films/sf-f and merged by scripts/merge.mjs into films/solar-system/film.json: edit the staging folders, never film.json. Rules: films/solar-system/conventions.md. Screenplay and facts: films/solar-system/screenplay.md.

lines: Drawn, animated and scored entirely in code. Voices: Gemini TTS.
Made with cinecode by Zakaria Fatahi · github.com/zakariaf/cinecode

score.note: The Saturn chapter's motif (wonder, Nell's question): six notes, so a cue's "motif": 6 states it in full, 3 or 4 hints it. Where it is stated: conventions.md, Music.

ganymede.name: Ganymede
ganymede.note: Part 7: true size (4 × 2634.1 / 71492), the biggest of the four.

titan.name: Titan
titan.note: Parts 0 and 8: Saturn's biggest moon at its true size (2.5 × 2574.7 / 60268).

uranus.name: Uranus
uranus.note: Part 9: on its side, rings upright (the preset's roll).

neptune.name: Neptune
neptune.note: Part 10: Neptune's true colour, a pale blue a shade bluer than Uranus (facts #96), passed over the engine preset (Voyager's boosted deep blue); the dark spot softened, its white cloud kept.

pluto.name: Pluto
pluto.note: Part 11, its pale heart toward us.

p06_rock_a.name: Far rock
p06_rock_a.note: Part 6 (6.2): one of two more asteroids, very far behind the first (z 6500), a speck. Stands in for the brief's debris n 4 'very far': debris can only lie within 0.35 of the lens behind the stage, so its four chunks came out as big as the asteroid, and its layout is seeded by film time (it would change at the merge).

p06_rock_b.name: Far rock
p06_rock_b.note: Part 6 (6.2): the other far asteroid (z 7500), a speck.

p05_phobos.name: Phobos
p05_phobos.note: Part 5 (5.2): Mars's bigger moon, a grey speck passing in front of Mars (z -250). Drawn about 8 times its true size (true: under 1 px) so the speck reads. Stands in for the brief's moonlets n 2: those two specks came out far from Mars and late (the second appears at 57% of the beat), and their layout is seeded by film time, so it would change at the merge.

p05_deimos.name: Deimos
p05_deimos.note: Part 5 (5.2): Mars's smaller moon, a speck passing behind Mars (z 300), hidden as it crosses the globe.

p09_orbitpin.name: Orbit pin
p09_orbitpin.note: Part 9 (9.2): an invisible stand-in at centre that the orbit beat is drawn through (its globe is 0.1 px), so Uranus rolls along a dotted path that stays put.

p11_kbo1.name: Icy world
p11_kbo1.note: Part 11: a far icy Kuiper Belt object (a speck at its distance), turning slowly. In place of debris, whose chunk sizes and depths come from the beat's film time (so they change in the merge) and can include a big near one.

p11_kbo2.name: Icy world
p11_kbo2.note: Part 11: a second icy speck; 11.2 flies past it.

scenes.note: Part 0, screenplay scene 1. Gran's hill at night. Blocking per conventions §5: telescope x 1990 facing left, its tube up-left at Saturn (the skydot at x 1290, y 230); Nell at 2150 and Gran at 2245 facing left; in 0.9 Nell steps to the eyepiece (2082) and Gran comes behind her (2170). 0.3 and 0.5 are Nell's view of the sky (Saturn's point at the centre, the stars round it twinkling). No figure's centre past x 2255 (the stone is painted at 2330-2510).

shots.note: screenplay 1.1. The hill under the Milky Way: the standing stone, two small figures and the telescope on the crest, Saturn's steady point up-left. No words: crickets, wind, the motif on celesta.
screenplay 1.2. Close on Nell against the sky: she looks up, then points up-left into the open sky.

camera.note: focus on a point left of and above Nell: she is framed alone against the sky (the telescope at the left), Gran (x 2245) out of frame at the right, the moon clear above her head

beats.text: Gran, what's that bright star?

beats.name: point
beats.note: started while the first point still holds, so the arm stays up

beats.name: point
beats.note: the third keeps it up to the cut to her view (0.3)

shots.note: screenplay 1.2 (insert). What Nell sees: Saturn's steady golden point among the stars. Twinkle: each star is a faint skydot (scene overlay, shots 0.3 and 0.5) that a run of short sunglow beats (2-4 frames each, random strength) flickers at about 4-6 Hz; Saturn's point stays steady. Generated; a shared twinkle effect could replace them.

camera.note: Nell's view up-left: Saturn's steady point at the centre of the frame, a few stars round it twinkling; the moon out of frame

shots.note: screenplay 1.3. Medium on Gran: she looks where Nell points and smiles; Nell asks from the left (O.S.).

beats.text: That's not a star, love. That's Saturn.
How can you tell?

shots.note: screenplay 1.3 (insert). Back to Nell's view: Saturn shines steady while the stars round it twinkle, under Gran's lesson (O.S.). Twinkle: each star is a faint skydot (scene overlay, shots 0.3 and 0.5) that a run of short sunglow beats (2-4 frames each, random strength) flickers at about 4-6 Hz; Saturn's point stays steady. Generated; a shared twinkle effect could replace them.

camera.note: Nell's view up-left: Saturn's steady point at the centre of the frame, a few stars round it twinkling; the moon out of frame

beats.text: See how it shines so steady? Stars twinkle. Planets don't.
beats.note: O.S. on the hill (she is just out of this view of the sky): vo so lint accepts an unseen speaker; the take is the same

shots.note: screenplay 1.4. Medium on Nell and Gran: she looks up at the steady point, then turns to Gran, eyes wide.

camera.note: a medium two-shot (it was a close on Nell with Gran's headless cardigan filling the right of the frame): Nell looks up from the sky to Gran's face. High angle, looking down on Nell as Gran does.

beats.text: A real planet? Can we go there?

shots.note: screenplay 1.5. Full on Nell, Gran and the telescope. Nell (left, facing right) and Gran (right, facing left) talk; Nell shrugs on 'But the Sun's gone.'

beats.text: Let's imagine we can. But let's go the long way round.
We'll start in the middle, with the Sun.
But the Sun's gone.

shots.note: screenplay 1.6. Medium on Gran. She turns to the open crest (face right), looks down and points at the ground: the Sun is down there, round the far side of the world (pointing this way keeps her hand clear of Nell's head). She turns back to Nell as she finishes, for Nell's O.S. line.

beats.text: It hasn't gone anywhere. The Earth spins, and right now our side is facing away from it.

beats.name: point
beats.note: point follows her look: down at the ground, steeper than point-down, and away from Nell

beats.text: So it's round the other side!

shots.note: screenplay 1.7. Full. Gran beckons toward the telescope; Nell steps up to the eyepiece (x 2082, facing left, eye level); Gran comes behind her (x 2170).

camera.note: offset: the same set-up as 0.7 (the stone whole at the right)

beats.text: Have a look.

scenes.note: Part 0, screenplay scene 2. Through the eyepiece: Saturn small at the centre, rings open, Titan a tiny orange dot beside it (true size). In 0.11 the eyepiece opens and the camera pans LEFT away from Saturn (the film's only inward move): Saturn slides out right, stars stream from a vanishing point at the left toward a small warm glow.

shots.note: screenplay 2.1. POV through the eyepiece.

beats.text: It's got rings!
Later. Sun first. Hold on tight.

shots.note: screenplay 2.2. The launch: the round view opens to the whole frame and the camera pans left, Saturn sliding out right; stars stream from the left (fx 0.15) where a small warm glow waits. The motif in full on strings. The last frame is the open flight toward the glow, the stream at full (Part 1 continues it).

beats.name: starstream
beats.note: fx and fy go in params: a beat field named fx is read as an fx beat (check: several beat kinds). The effect plays its own wind-swell at its start.

beats.text: We're flying!

lint.note: the POV through the eyepiece continues across the cut on purpose (screenplay 2.1 to 2.2): 0.11 opens the round view from the same framing, then pans away

scenes.note: Part 1, The Sun (screenplay scene 3). The Sun (scale 7) at centre with its living face (sunface) and a soft glow (sunglow who: sun, a 0.25, so the face and the row of Earths stay readable); Earth at true size beside it (earth_speck, a blue speck) at east. Comes in on a cut from Part 0's flight (0.9): the stars are still streaming as the Sun swells. The narrator's first words in the film.

overlays.name: sunface
overlays.note: the Sun's boiling face, spots and prominences; a scene overlay so it is drawn before (under) the sizerow row of Earths in 1.2

overlays.name: sunglow
overlays.note: the Sun's light on its own disc; a 0.25 (sunface header: at 1 its white core turns the face and the row white)

overlays.name: skydot
overlays.note: a crumb: Mercury, grey, nearest the Sun

overlays.name: skydot
overlays.note: Earth's blue glint on its true-size speck, big enough that the eye finds "that little dot" (and the blue crumb in 1.5)

shots.note: screenplay 3.1. Cut in from 0.9's flight: the Sun opens where 0.9 left its glow (left, about x 0.2, y 0.45) with the stars still streaming from it, and the camera pans and flies in together (0-5 s) until the Sun fills the middle of the frame, its face churning. A swell sting. The gag ("Older than Gran!" / "Only just.") lands on the full face.

lint.note: the flight in: the dolly brings the Sun from small to filling the frame on purpose

beats.text: This is the Sun. It's a star: our very own star.
It's so bright!
It's about four and a half billion years old.
Older than Gran!
Only just.

beats.name: starstream
beats.note: still streaming from the cut (it builds over its first 0.6 s), dying away by 3 s; the vanishing point on the Sun

beats.name: starstream
beats.note: editor (join 0.9 → 1.1): the same streaks as the beat above (same shot, name and start, so the same seed), at full by the 3rd frame and gone by 0.45 s while the 3 s stream builds, so the flight doesn't blink off at the cut

shots.note: screenplay 3.2 (first part). The camera flies back (z 800 → −900) until the whole Sun sits left of centre and Earth, a blue speck at true size with its glint, floats at the right. "That little dot." gets a beat to itself; then 109 Earths race across the Sun's middle like beads (sizerow) on "a hundred times wider"; cut once the row is complete.

lint.note: the dolly back from the Sun's face; Earth is a true-size speck beside it on purpose

beats.text: Where's Earth?
That little dot.
beats.note: the screenplay's line "That little dot. The Sun is about a hundred times wider than Earth." in two beats (critics, round 6): a 0.8 s look at the dot before the comparison; same words

beats.text: The Sun is about a hundred times wider than Earth.

beats.name: sizerow
beats.note: 109 Earths across the Sun (facts #6), starting on "a hundred times wider"; scope scene so the row carries on whole across the cut into 1.3 (the close-up of the row); its dur ends exactly at 1.3's cut (set by script from the plan)

shots.note: screenplay 3.2 (second part). Cut in on the row at the Sun's east edge: Earths about 20 px across, a long line of them across the boiling face, ending at the limb; black space at the right and below, so the captions read. The Sun stays at the left.

lint.note: a close-up of the row of Earths at the Sun's edge: a crop of the Sun on purpose

beats.text: It would take more than a million Earths to fill it up.
That's a lot of Earths.

shots.note: screenplay 3.3. A crop into the Sun's east edge: the bright rim and its prominence against black, the surface boiling; slow push-in. The disc fills only the left third, so the Sun stays at the left and both captions sit on black.

lint.note: a crop into the Sun's edge on purpose

beats.text: Its surface is about five and a half thousand degrees Celsius. And its middle is fifteen million.
My bath is only forty!
beats.note: tone "amazed" → "delighted" (critics, round 6: the amazed take rose like a question)

shots.note: screenplay 3.4. A slow pan from the Sun's blazing edge out to the right; it ends with the Sun's limb still a great curve at the left of the frame and the crumbs beside it: Mercury (grey), Venus (cream), Earth (its blue glint) and Mars (red), small points next to the huge Sun.

lint.note: the Sun's limb is cut by the left edge on purpose (its great curve beside the crumbs); the worlds are true-size specks and points of light

beats.text: Almost all the stuff in our solar system is in the Sun: ninety-nine point eight percent.
The planets are just the crumbs.

shots.note: screenplay 3.5. Wide and still: the Sun at the left, Earth's speck at the right. The narrator says the real Earth is much farther away (critics, round 6: the picture shows true sizes, not the distance); then light leaves the Sun's limb and travels across the dark to Earth on "eight minutes". Ends the part: held after "Never ever. I promise."

lint.note: Earth is a true-size speck beside the Sun on purpose

beats.text: The real Earth is much farther away: more than a hundred Suns in a row.
beats.note: NEW line (critics, round 6), not in the screenplay: proposed fact row in the team B report (Earth–Sun 150 million km / the Sun's 1.4 million km = 107). Remove this beat if the director declines it.

beats.text: Its light reaches Earth in about eight minutes. And Earth goes once round the Sun every year.

beats.name: lightpulse
beats.note: sunlight on its way to Earth, leaving the Sun's right limb at Earth's height, timed to "reaches Earth in about eight minutes" (facts #10)

beats.text: I've been round eight times. I'm eight!
And remember, love: never look at the Sun through a telescope. Never ever.
Never ever. I promise.

scenes.note: Part 2, Mercury (screenplay scene 4). From Mercury the Sun is a huge glow cut by the frame's left edge (sunglow x −0.12, y 0.4, r 0.31: the ladder). Mercury (scale 1.2) races left to right; then the orrery race of laps; then a crop across its terminator.

shots.note: screenplay 4.1. Mercury already racing in from the left as the part cuts in; it keeps running left to right through the whole shot while the camera pans after it (slower than Mercury, so it always gains on the frame); a whoosh as it passes the middle. Its orbit draws in round the Sun at the left on "round the Sun" (orbit side −1).

beats.text: Mercury: the smallest planet, only a little bigger than our Moon. And the closest to the Sun.
It's so fast!
The fastest of all. It whizzes round the Sun in just eighty-eight days.

beats.name: sunglow
beats.note: the Sun from Mercury: about 2.6 times as big as from Earth (facts #15, the ladder)
as Mercury races in from the left

beats.name: orbit
beats.note: Mercury's orbit round the Sun at the left, drawn once it has settled

shots.note: screenplay 4.2. The orrery, full frame: Mercury's small orbit and Earth's, seen from above; Earth goes round 8 times while Mercury laps it; the counters tick to 8 and 33 and stop together on "thirty-three". The camera frames an empty point so no actor is in frame.

beats.text: So how old would I be on Mercury?
You're eight in Earth years. In Mercury years, you'd be thirty-three.
beats.note: tone added (critics, round 6): the plain take rose on "Earth years?" like a question

beats.text: Thirty-three! I'm a grown-up!
You'd still go to bed at eight.

beats.name: orrery
beats.note: 8 Earth years: Earth 8 laps, Mercury 33 (facts #16); the laps stop together on "thirty-three"

shots.note: screenplay 4.3. A crop of Mercury, grey and cratered: the day side lit at the left, the night side dark at the right; the camera drifts slowly across the line between them. Ends the part, held after the last line.

lint.note: a crop across Mercury's terminator on purpose

beats.note: at the cut (unseen): the preset craters read as white domes this close, so they are swapped for ringed spots (a pale rim round a darker floor), spread all round the globe; spin 0 so the surface holds still (Mercury turns once in 59 days) and this frame is the same wherever the part lands in the film

beats.text: With almost no air to hold in the heat, its days reach four hundred and thirty degrees, and its nights drop to minus one hundred and eighty.
I'd need my scarf and my sun hat.

beats.name: sunglow
beats.note: the Sun's blaze at the left edge, as from Mercury (the ladder), warming the day side

scenes.note: Part 3, Venus (screenplay scene 5). Venus at the centre; Earth's twin glides in beside it in 3.2 and is put away at the cut to 3.3; the dive into the clouds (clouddive) in 3.3; Venus alone with its orbit in 3.4. Sunglow x -0.04, r 0.17 (conventions 3).

shots.note: screenplay 5.1. Full on Venus, the slow push already moving from the first frame: a smooth, creamy, glowing globe. Gran remembers the evening star.

beats.text: Ah, Venus. When I was little, I called her the evening star.
But she's not a star, Gran!
Quite right.
After the Moon, Venus is the brightest thing in our night sky.

shots.note: screenplay 5.2. Wide, static: Venus left of centre; Earth glides in from the right to sit beside it, nearly the same size (Venus = 0.949 Earth; earth_twin 2.53 vs venus 2.4).

beats.text: It's almost the same size as Earth. Some call it Earth's twin.
Could we live there?

shots.note: screenplay 5.3. The dive: a push-in (zoom 1 -> 4) with the camera flying in (z 0 -> 1200) until cream cloud fills the frame; the cloud darkens toward ochre and a deep orange glow rises from below (clouddive). A low rumble under it (wind-swell; the engine's 'hum' is a person humming a tune).

beats.note: a low rumble rising through the dive; ends (with its release) at 23.2 s, inside the shot

beats.text: Not a chance. Under those thick clouds, it's the hottest planet of all. Hot enough to melt lead.
Hotter than Mercury?
Hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. The longest a robot probe lasted down there was just over two hours.
Oh, poor robots.

shots.note: screenplay 5.4. Wide: Venus alone again, its bands drifting the 'wrong' way (spin -0.05, set on the first beat only: a spin change mid-shot makes the bands jump), its dotted orbit drawing round the Sun at the left (side -1). Ends the part: held after 'Nice try.'

beats.text: And Venus spins backwards. There, the Sun rises in the west.
And Venus spins so slowly that one turn takes longer than its whole year!
So I'd get a birthday every day!
Nice try.

scenes.note: Part 4, Earth (screenplay scene 6). Earth at the centre, the Moon small beyond (far_east, z 2400). Earth's night half (nightside, from the sunglow's point at the left) and in it, at the lower right, a warm point: Gran's hill. The motif on flute.

shots.note: screenplay 6.1. Wide, slow dolly in (z -600 -> 300) already moving: the blue Earth turning, clouds over it, the Moon small beyond. The flute states the motif.

beats.text: There's us!
Earth: the third planet from the Sun. Our home.

shots.note: screenplay 6.2. Full on Earth, static: the lit side at the left, the dark side at the right, and on it the tiny warm point (Gran's hill).

beats.text: It's the only place we know of with living things. And about seventy-one percent of its surface is ocean.
And that's our side, in the dark!

scenes.note: Part 4, the cut home (screenplay scene 7): the only mid-journey cut to the hill. Blocking as conventions 5: telescope 1990, Nell at the eyepiece 2082, Gran right behind her 2170; Saturn's skydot up-left. Crickets only.

shots.note: screenplay 7.1. Medium on Nell and Gran, static. Nell keeps her eye to the eyepiece and waves up at the sky with her free hand; Gran, right behind her, smiles.

beats.text: Hello, Gran! I can see you from up here!

beats.note: a laugh on her face only: the laugh gesture's hands land on Nell's head at this distance

beats.text: I'm right behind you, love.

beats.note: Nell keeps her eye to the eyepiece: an explicit look ends the listener glance up at Gran (which starts 0.05-0.3 s into the line)

beats.text: You know, every other planet is named after a god. Earth just means 'the ground'.

beats.note: Nell keeps her eye to the eyepiece: an explicit look ends the listener glance up at Gran (which starts 0.05-0.3 s into the line)

scenes.note: Part 4, the Moon (screenplay scene 8). 4.4: the Earth-Moon row (true distance, 29 Earths; the three globes' centres on one line, y 970). 4.5: the Moon alone, close (moon_big placed at the cut); split at Gran's line: the hill (p04d, 4.6) and the Moon again (p04e, 4.7).

moon_big.note: off the frame in 4.4; placed at the centre at the cut to 4.5

shots.note: screenplay 8.1. Wide, static, the two at the frame's edges: Earth at the left, the Moon a grey speck at the right, at true size and true distance (60.3 Earth radii). Earths pop in one by one, edge to edge, 29 of them (sizerow on the invisible stand-in earth_gap, ratio 50).

beats.text: Is the Moon far?
About thirty Earths could fit in a row between us and the Moon.

beats.note: the group ends on the 29th pop (9.26 s after the line starts); its Earth is full size 0.22 s later

shots.note: screenplay 8.2 (first part). Full on the Moon (moon_big, scale 2), grey and cratered; a slow push in from the first frame while Nell asks and the narrator answers. Cut on the end of the line to Gran on the hill (4.6).

beats.text: Has anyone been there?
Twelve people have walked on it. And in 2026, four astronauts flew all the way around it.
beats.tts: Twelve people have walked on it. And in twenty twenty-six, four astronauts flew all the way around it.

scenes.note: Part 4, back on the hill for Gran's memory (screenplay 8.2, split at Gran's line): the Moon's music carries on under it (no cue), crickets. Blocking as 4.3 / conventions 5: telescope 1990, Nell at the eyepiece 2082, Gran right behind her 2170; Saturn's skydot up-left.

gran.note: turned from the telescope to the real Moon, up-right in the hill's night sky, from the cut

shots.note: screenplay 8.2 (Gran's memory). Medium on Gran behind Nell, static. Gran stands turned to the real Moon up-right in the night sky and remembers, smiling; Nell keeps her eye to the eyepiece and says she'll go. Gran turns back to her as she speaks, amused, and nods.

beats.text: I watched the first moonwalk on a tiny television.

beats.note: Nell keeps her eye to the eyepiece: an explicit look ends the listener glance up at Gran

beats.text: I'm going there. I'll jump really high.

scenes.note: Part 4, the Moon again (screenplay 8.2, after the hill): a new framing, a crop of its lit limb; at 'drifts farther away' the Moon eases back (z 0 -> 300) and Nell calls after it. Ends the part, held after 'Come back, Moon!'. The wonder cue carries on (no cue).

shots.note: screenplay 8.2 (last part). A crop of the Moon's lit upper-left limb against the dark, static; the Moon drifts back (z 0 -> 300) on the four centimetres line, its edge pulling away. Held after the last line (part end).

beats.text: You would. On the Moon, you'd weigh only a sixth as much.
And every year, the Moon drifts about four centimetres farther away.
Come back, Moon!

scenes.note: Part 5, Mars (screenplay scene 9). Mars (cast scale 2.2) at centre; the mars preset already spins 0.08, so its features drift at 0.08 from 5.1 on and never jump at a cut. The Sun's glow at the left (x 0, y 0.4, r 0.08: conventions 3) in the wide and full shots; the crop (5.3) leaves it out.

shots.note: screenplay 9.1. A short starstream (vanishing point just right of centre) while the camera starts to fly; then Mars, a small red ball, swims up out of the dark as the dolly carries us in (z -1700 -> 400, eased, at rest before the narrator's line ends). The running gag: are we nearly at Saturn?

beats.text: Are we nearly at Saturn?
Not even close. This is Mars.
The red planet. It's red because its dusty ground is full of rust.

shots.note: screenplay 9.2. Full on Mars, turning (spin 0.08, the preset's, from the shot start); its two tiny moons go round it as two specks, Phobos passing in front (left to right) and Deimos behind (right to left, hidden as it crosses): two small planet actors (p05_phobos, p05_deimos), deterministic, in place of moonlets n 2, moved by one place a frame (round 7: a planet moved with walk/run/enter gets the engine's automatic footsteps; a place makes no sound). Framed a little looser than full (zoom 0.82) so the moons stay in frame either side. Nell's checklist: could I live here?

beats.note: Phobos passes in front of Mars, left to right, just below the equator, and on out of frame: one place a frame (the path of the old run beat, speed 3.4), so no footsteps
Deimos passes behind Mars, right to left, a little higher, hidden as it crosses the globe: one place a frame (the old run, speed 3.7)

beats.text: Could I live on Mars?
It's about half as wide as Earth. A day there is only a little longer than ours. But the air is thin, and mostly carbon dioxide. You couldn't breathe it.

shots.note: screenplay 9.3. A crop of Mars's upper-right limb (zoom 2.8, focus [0.85, 0.3]): the camera glides low along the limb (a tilt-up, from below the focus up toward the polar cap, with a slow dolly in, z 0 -> 400) over rust-red ground, a dark patch and Olympus Mons (round 7: a pale shield ringed by its dark scarp, a double caldera, at 18.6 N, a set at the cut with spin 0 so it is in view for the whole glide and sits there in the merged film too). Olympus Mons and the robots.

beats.note: the moons out of the crop and the wide (off every later view)

Olympus Mons at its true size and place: the pale shield 585 km across (w 0.086 = 292 / 3396 km), ringed by its darker scarp, a double caldera (drawn a little big), at about 19 N (NASA Photojournal: 'Olympus Mons is also wider (585 km, 363 miles) than the state of Arizona'), on the limb the glide passes. spin 0 at the cut: the spin phase is film time x spin, so with Mars turning the volcano would sit somewhere else once the film is merged (as 2.3 does for Mercury's craters).

beats.text: It has the biggest volcano in the solar system: Olympus Mons. It's almost three times as tall as Mount Everest.
Are there any Martians?
Only robots. Mars is the only planet we know of where everyone is a robot.

shots.note: screenplay 9.4. Wide: Mars small at the right, the Sun's glow at the left; Mars's dotted orbit draws itself in round the Sun (side -1) as the camera eases back a little; at rest well before the cut. Nell does the age sum herself; Gran's tease ends the part, held.

beats.note: Mars turns again in the wide (a new spin only at a cut).

beats.text: A year on Mars is 687 days. Nearly two of ours.
beats.tts: A year on Mars is six hundred and eighty-seven days. Nearly two of ours.

beats.text: So on Mars, I'd be four?
Just over four.
Four again. Heaven help us.

scenes.note: Part 6, the asteroid belt (screenplay scene 10): the film's one action scene, which turns out to be nothing. The asteroid (cast: mercury paint, ob 0.62, roll 0.5, scale 0.5) waits far ahead at z 3000 for 6.1-6.2 and is placed at z 0 at the cut to 6.3. The Sun's glow (x 0.02, y 0.4, r 0.045: conventions 3) in every shot.

shots.note: screenplay 10.1. Mid-rush from the first frame: the camera (handheld) flies forward from z -1500 through a storm of rocks (debris n 160, ice 0.2, speed 1.8) streaking past the lens, still flying fast at the hard cut (z about 500 there: the move's window runs 1.3 x the shot toward 700; flown on to 1500 the storm thinned to a few rocks before the cut), whooshes left and right; chase music on the downbeat. The asteroid is a far speck ahead.

beats.note: a mottled grey rock: darker patches that turn with it and fewer craters than Mercury's paint (whose many crater highlights read as white blisters up close in 6.3)

beats.name: debris
beats.note: the same rocks as the next beat (same shot, name and start, so the same seed), built up in 0.12 s so the storm is there from the first frames; it fades out while the long beat is at full

beats.name: debris
beats.note: dur past the shot so it never thins out before the hard cut

beats.text: Rocks! Hold on, Gran!

shots.note: screenplay 10.2. Hard cut: the music stops dead on a plunk. Wide, static, almost empty: far off, the one asteroid turns slowly; two more rocks drift, tiny and far. A silent beat, then the narrator, amused: 'Don't worry.' and Nell's sheepish answer straight after the scare (round 7: the punchline moved up from 6.3), then the facts. dur = the last line's end + a 2.4 s hold (a fixed dur: the drift's place beats would otherwise push the hold past them).

beats.note: two more rocks, very far (z 6500, 7500), drifting slowly right to left: a place every 3 frames (0.3 px on screen), so no footsteps

beats.text: Don't worry.
Oh. I was holding my breath.
This is the asteroid belt, between Mars and Jupiter. There are millions of rocks here, left over from when the solar system was made.

shots.note: screenplay 10.3. Full on the one asteroid (placed at z 0 at the cut): egg-shaped, grey and cratered, turning slowly in the dark while the camera drifts round it (it slides slowly left across the frame). Mystery, quiet; a quiet look before the narrator. dur = the last line's end + a 1.8 s hold (the part's end: at least 0.8 s after the last line; a fixed dur because the slide's place beats would otherwise push the hold past them).

beats.note: the asteroid slides slowly left (1.3 px/s, the old walk speed 0.068): a place a frame, so no hop, land or footsteps

beats.text: But space is so big that they're very far apart. The big ones are, on average, nearly eight times farther apart than Earth and the Moon.
Put them all together, and they'd still weigh less than our Moon. Spacecraft travel through quite safely.

scenes.note: Part 7, Jupiter (screenplay scene 11). Jupiter (scale 4) rises to `centre` in 7.1. Earth (earth_spot, true size) and the four Galilean moons (true sizes) are offstage until their shots bring them in.

shots.note: screenplay 11.1. Out of the dark below, Jupiter rises (a slow glide up to centre) and swells as the camera dollies in (z -1500 -> 600) until it fills two-thirds of the frame. Triumph on the downbeat and a swell.

lint.note: the dolly: Jupiter rises from below the frame and grows to two-thirds of the frame on purpose; its lower limb rises through the bottom edge as it comes up (about 0.5 s)

beats.text: Is that Saturn?
Not yet. This is Jupiter, the biggest planet of all. If it were hollow, about a thousand Earths could fit inside.

shots.note: screenplay 11.2. A crop of the Great Red Spot (22 S, turned to face us); a small blue Earth (true size) drifts in from the left at z -50 and stops beside it: smaller than the storm. Framed so the spot and Earth sit about a third down and the south limb stays above the bottom caption band (the captions sit on black space).

lint.note: a crop of the Great Red Spot: Jupiter fills and overflows the frame on purpose

beats.note: at the cut: the spot faces us and stays put whatever the film time

beats.text: What's that red spot? An eye?
A storm. A giant storm, bigger than Earth, that has been raging for hundreds of years.

shots.note: screenplay 11.3. Full on Jupiter; the bands race round (spin 0.4, set on the shot's first beat so nothing jumps).

lint.note: Earth leaves the picture at the cut: it is put away behind the globe (hidden for the whole shot), so no jump is seen

beats.note: Earth put away behind the globe

beats.text: And it spins faster than any other planet. A day on Jupiter lasts only about ten hours.
That's how long I sleep!

shots.note: screenplay 11.4. POV through the eyepiece (r 0.36, centred on Jupiter, as 0.8): Jupiter a small striped disc, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto (true sizes) in a line along its equator, two each side, each a bright pinpoint. Wonder, the motif hinted on celesta.

lint.note: the eyepiece view: Jupiter small in the round field with its four moons, as from the hill

beats.note: Jupiter far back: the camera cannot go wider than the whole set, so depth makes it small

beats.name: sunglow
beats.note: a pinpoint of light on Ganymede (its place with Jupiter centred), not the Sun

beats.name: sunglow
beats.note: a pinpoint of light on Io (its place with Jupiter centred), not the Sun

beats.name: sunglow
beats.note: a pinpoint of light on Europa (its place with Jupiter centred), not the Sun

beats.name: sunglow
beats.note: a pinpoint of light on Callisto (its place with Jupiter centred), not the Sun

beats.text: It has more than a hundred moons. The four biggest were first seen in 1610, by Galileo, with one of the very first telescopes.
beats.tts: It has more than a hundred moons. The four biggest were first seen in sixteen ten, by Galileo, with one of the very first telescopes.

beats.text: And with your telescope, you can see those four from our hill.
Tomorrow night!
One of them, Ganymede, is the biggest moon of all. It's even bigger than the planet Mercury.

shots.note: screenplay 11.5, re-staged (critics, round 7): the eyepiece opens; Jupiter and its moons fade as the orrery race fades in, a callback to 2.2: Earth and Jupiter round the Sun, seen from above, with lap counters; Jupiter's counter reaches 1 as Nell says "Twelve years", Earth's shows 11. Playful.

lint.note: opens on the same framing as 7.4 on purpose: the eyepiece view widens out of it (screenplay 11.5), then Jupiter fades into the orrery map (no planet in frame after 2 s)

beats.note: Earth, parked behind Jupiter since 7.3, goes before Jupiter turns see-through

beats.name: orrery
beats.note: 11.9 Earth years: Earth 11 laps, Jupiter 1 (4333 days, facts: about twelve of our years). Jupiter's counter pops to 1 at the start of "Twelve years for one cake?" while Earth's shows 11 (Gran's "nearly twelve"); run and dur are timed to the voiced lines.

beats.text: One trip round the Sun takes Jupiter about twelve of our years.
So your first Jupiter birthday is when you're nearly twelve.
Twelve years for one cake?
One very big cake.

scenes.note: Part 8, Saturn (screenplay scene 12; the chapter's s02, restaged). Saturn (2.5) at centre, far ahead at the start of 8.1 and at z 0 from its arrival; Titan (0.107, true size) in front of the stage near the camera's axis for the flight in, then put away behind the globe.

shots.note: screenplay 12.1 (round 7: the narrator's line is Gran's "And now it's later.", the payoff of her "Later. Sun first." in 0.8). The camera flies (z -1500 -> 1000) toward a small golden point ahead, which opens into Saturn with its rings; Titan swings past the left edge. The motif in full on strings on the downbeat, at 0.65; a wind-swell.

lint.note: the flight: Saturn grows from a golden point to the full planet on purpose

beats.text: Saturn! At last!

beats.note: the arrival: wonder at 0.65 (as the scene cue, so it merges): the statement of the motif is the loud moment

beats.text: It's got rings!
And now it's later.

shots.note: screenplay 12.2. Wide, static: the small Sun at the left, Saturn small on the right; a shaft of sunlight (lightbeam, from the sunglow's point) reaches Saturn and lights it.

beats.note: Titan put away behind the globe (the moonlets draw their own Titan in 8.7)

beats.name: lightbeam
beats.note: reaches Saturn at about 5.8 s and is full at 7.4 s; its fade (the beat's last 6%) falls after the cut

beats.text: Is it far from the Sun?
So far that sunlight takes about eighty minutes to get here.

shots.note: screenplay 12.3. Full on Saturn, static; nine Earths pop in across its middle (sizerow, true scale).

beats.text: Is it big?
Nine times wider than Earth.

beats.name: sizerow
beats.note: the ninth Earth pops at 2.9 s; the row stays to the cut (1.2 s after the ninth)

shots.note: screenplay 12.4 (round 7: the drift stops short of the clouds). A crop of Saturn: the globe big and high, its top cut, the rings across its lower half, black space below them where the captions sit; the camera drifts in toward the cloud bands (z 0 -> 600) and the last frame still holds the banded globe and the rings.

lint.note: a crop of Saturn on purpose: the globe's top and both ends of the rings are out of frame while the camera drifts in toward the bands

beats.name: clouddive
beats.note: texture only (the critics: no dive into cloud, Venus 3.3 does that): billows on the bands as the camera drifts in

beats.text: Could I stand on it?
No. Saturn has no solid ground. It's mostly hydrogen and helium.
It's so light for its size, it would float in a bath.
We'd need a really big bath.

shots.note: screenplay 12.5. The rings' edge, close (a crop), speckled with ice and rock (ringfield); the camera flies in and chunks open out past the lens.

lint.note: a crop into the rings' edge; the camera flies in through the ring pieces, so Saturn is mostly out of frame on purpose

beats.text: What are the rings made of?
Billions of chunks of ice and rock: some as small as dust, some as big as a house.

shots.note: screenplay 12.6. Full, static: the camera sinks to the ring plane; Saturn's tilt eases 0.38 -> 0.012 over 3 s (a `set` a frame, generated) and the rings close to a thin bright line across the globe.

beats.text: And the main rings are only about ten metres thick.

shots.note: screenplay 12.7 (round 7: framed at full, not wide, so Titan is drawn at its true size against Saturn). The same framing as 8.6: the camera rises out of the ring plane again (tilt 0.012 -> 0.38 over 1.25 s, a set a frame) and the rings open, then small moons appear one by one, faster and faster, the far ones passing behind (moonlets, Titan at true size).

beats.text: Does it have a moon?

beats.name: moonlets
beats.note: Saturn's globe is about 347 px in radius here, so Titan at bigR 0.044 is drawn at its true size (15 px, facts #69), above the two-small-moon floor; bigX, bigY keep it in frame, upper right past the ring tip

beats.text: Hundreds! More than any other planet.

lint.note: the same framing as 8.6 on purpose: 8.6 sinks the camera to the ring plane, 8.7 rises out of it again (the rings reopen from the edge-on line), one continuous movement across the cut

shots.note: screenplay 12.8 (round 7: Nell's "How far does it go, Gran?" and Gran's "Let's find out. Hold on tight." added, the question that pulls the second half; answered by Part 11). Wide: the Sun's small glow at the left; the camera pulls back through depth as Saturn's dotted orbit draws itself; at rest before the last lines.

lint.note: the camera pulls back through depth: Saturn and its orbit shrink toward the end

beats.text: And one year on Saturn lasts about twenty-nine Earth years.
So on Saturn, I'm not even one!
How far does it go, Gran?
Let's find out. Hold on tight.

scenes.note: Part 9, Uranus (screenplay scene 13). Gran tells the Herschel story, which turns out to be Nell's own. Uranus at scale 2: a far pale dot that the long dolly of 9.1 grows into a small globe (it comes in from z 20000), then at z 0 from 9.2. The far Sun one bright star at the left (sunglow r 0.006).

shots.note: screenplay 13.1. A long, slow dolly through the dark from the cut (camera z -1500 → 1500 over the whole shot, and Uranus drifting in from z 20000): far ahead a pale blue-green dot, still a dot while Gran says "a little dot", grows into a small globe as the narrator says it was a planet.

beats.text: In 1781, a man called William Herschel was looking through his telescope, just like you.
beats.tts: In seventeen eighty-one, a man called William Herschel was looking through his telescope, just like you.

beats.text: He spotted a little dot, and thought it was a comet, or a star.
Just like me and Saturn!
It was a planet: Uranus. The first planet ever found with a telescope.
He wanted to name it after the King. King George.
Planet George!

beats.note: Uranus comes in through depth over the shot (with the dolly: about 10 times bigger by the end); ends before the last line does, so it never sets the shot length

shots.note: screenplay 13.2. Full on Uranus (now at z 0): tipped on its side, rings standing up round it like a hoop; it rolls slowly down along its dotted orbit (the orbit pinned to an invisible stand-in at centre, so the path stays put), its clouds turning.

beats.text: Why is it so blue?
A gas called methane. And look: Uranus is tipped right over. It rolls around the Sun on its side, like a ball.

shots.note: screenplay 13.3. A crop of Uranus: the lit side against the shadow; a slow push into the dark half, ending with the frame mostly dark (then the cut home to the hill, 9.4). Playful for the scarf.

lint.note: the push into the dark half slides Uranus's limb out past the left edge: it grazes the edge for half a second on its way out

beats.text: So parts of it have a winter twenty-one years long, in the dark.
Twenty-one years of winter?
Better pack a bigger scarf.

scenes.note: Part 9, a wordless cut home (added after the round-6 critics; no screenplay shot): Nell and Gran have been off screen since 4.3, and the dawn lines need a sign that the night is going on and Nell is tiring. Blocking as 4.3 (conventions 5): telescope 1990, Nell at the eyepiece 2082, Gran behind her 2170; Saturn's skydot up-left. Crickets only.

shots.note: added (round-6 critics), no screenplay shot. Medium on Nell at the eyepiece with Gran behind her, static, wordless: Nell, eye to the eyepiece, goes sleepy and yawns behind her hands; Gran looks down at her and smiles. Crickets, then the cut to black into Neptune.

beats.name: gasp
beats.note: a yawn: both hands up to her mouth, the sleepy face kept (the gasp only swaps a neutral or happy face for surprise)

scenes.note: Part 10, Neptune (screenplay scene 14): the quietest part. Neptune at scale 2 in its true pale colour (skeleton params). Near silence for 3 s as it lifts out of black, then mystery 0.2. "transition": "cut": it now follows the hill (9.4), and the fade up from black is the shot's own.

shots.note: screenplay 14.1. Out of black (fadeIn 3), near silence under a faint wind bed: a pale blue globe a shade bluer than Uranus, the far Sun one bright star at the left, which Nell names.

beats.note: a faint bed under the silence, so it is not digital zero

beats.text: Look, Gran. The Sun's just a little star now.
beats.note: changed from the screenplay ("It's so dark out here.") at the round-6 critics' request: it names the shrinking Sun at its last step and calls back to 1.1

beats.text: Neptune: the farthest planet. Sunlight takes four hours to get here.

shots.note: screenplay 14.2. A crop of Neptune: white methane clouds streaking fast across the pale blue (spin from the cut; the skeleton's spot and cloud plus a few white streaks). Zoom 2.2, not the screenplay's 2.6 (the limb's ink segments showed at 2.6), and focus 0.8 low on the globe so its bottom limb sits at about 0.77 of the frame and the caption sits on dark sky below it; the streak that rode the upper limb moved from lat 0.42 to 0.3

beats.text: It's the windiest planet. Its winds blow faster than two thousand kilometres an hour.

shots.note: screenplay 14.3. Wide, static: Neptune small at the right, its dotted orbit drawing very slowly toward the far Sun; a silent beat at the end.

beats.text: You can't see Neptune with just your eyes. People found it with sums first.
One year here is a hundred and sixty-five of ours. Since it was discovered, Neptune has been round the Sun only once.
Not even Gran is that old.
Thank you, love.

scenes.note: Part 11, Pluto, the Kuiper Belt and how big it all is (screenplay scene 15). Pluto (1.4) at centre, its heart toward us (spin 0 from the cut, so the heart does not depend on the film time); Charon (0.71) at east, z 300. The belt is almost empty space near Pluto: two far icy specks (p11_kbo1, p11_kbo2), crowded only on the orrery (11.3). Then the great zoom out, and the smallest picture in the film.

shots.note: screenplay 15.1. Almost empty dark, a far icy speck or two; a small pale world comes in out of depth ahead and grows into its place over the first 5.5 s, its bright heart facing us, Charon beside it; then a slow drift in.

beats.note: Pluto comes in out of depth from far ahead and grows into its place
Charon with it

beats.text: Look! That one's got a heart!
That's Pluto: a dwarf planet, smaller than our Moon.
And it was named by a girl of eleven, at breakfast with her grandad.
A girl named a planet?
She did.

lint.note: Pluto arrives out of depth (z 4500 to 0 over the first 5.5 s, the critics' fix) and the slow dolly goes on growing it: it is under a wide shot's size for the first 10 s on purpose; Charon beside it keeps the shot wide

shots.note: screenplay 15.2. The camera flies on through near-empty dark (z -1200 → 1500, its axis well right of Pluto): a far speck passes; Pluto and Charon fall behind at the left (outward is left to right), then are faded out off frame.

beats.text: Pluto lives in the Kuiper Belt: a huge ring of icy worlds out past Neptune. There may be millions of them.

beats.note: off frame by now: gone before the orrery

shots.note: screenplay 15.3. The orrery, full frame, zooming out (au 1.6 → 60) as the narrator speaks: the Sun and the inner orbits, out past the giants to Pluto's tilted oval and the misty Kuiper Belt by "reach Pluto"; three years pass, so the inner planets visibly go round.

beats.text: On average, sunlight takes about five and a half hours to reach Pluto.
And the spacecraft Voyager 1 is out even farther. So far that its messages take a whole day to get home.

shots.note: screenplay 15.4. The orrery pulls out and fades into the starfield as the camera keeps pulling back; the Sun shrinks to one star among thousands at the left, the Milky Way's band across the frame.

beats.name: orrery
beats.note: ends at 9.5 s, nearly gone by "Where's home?"; its last frame draws the Sun exactly as the sunglow that takes over

beats.name: sunglow
beats.note: the far Sun after the orrery has faded (same place and size as its last frame and as 11.5)

beats.text: And our Sun is just one of more than a hundred billion stars in our galaxy.
Where's home?
beats.note: tone: the screenplay says quiet; [small, bright, quiet] was read aloud twice, so hushed

scenes.note: Part 11, the pale blue dot (screenplay 15.5) on its own set: the space kit with a faint Milky Way (milky 0.3), a dark patch of sky so the one blue point is the thing to find. Silence (a faint wind bed), then the motif on music-box. The sunglow and the paleray keep drawing through the dissolve into 12.1.

shots.note: screenplay 15.5. Wide, static, very still, a dark patch of sky: the far Sun a star at the left; a faint scattered ray of light across the black, and in it one pale blue point. Silence, then the motif on music-box. The ray keeps drawing through the dissolve into Part 12.

beats.note: a faint bed under the silence, so it is not digital zero

beats.name: paleray
beats.note: scope scene on purpose (conventions §4): the ray and dot keep drawing through the 0.8 s dissolve into 12.1. The dot (size 4, the only clearly blue point in the frame) fades up over 0.5 s from 14.45 s, so it is there on the word "point" (about 14.6 s); the ray a little brighter (a 0.22) against the faint Milky Way of p11_space

beats.text: In 1990, from far past Neptune, Voyager 1 looked back one last time and took a picture of home.
beats.tts: In nineteen ninety, from far past Neptune, Voyager 1 looked back one last time and took a picture of home.

beats.text: Earth was a single point of light.
That's us?
That's us. Everyone we've ever loved is on that little dot.

scenes.note: Part 12, screenplay scene 16 (night). Dissolve in from Part 11's pale blue dot. Nell at the eyepiece (2082, facing left), Gran behind her (2170). 12.2 is the silent time-lapse from night to dawn as they sit (Nell 2110 facing right, Gran 2215 facing left).

shots.note: screenplay 16.1. Close on Nell at the eyepiece: she straightens, turns right and looks up at Gran. Crickets first.

camera.note: close on Nell at the eyepiece (Gran's cardigan a soft dark edge at the right), easing back to a medium two-shot as she steps back and turns, so Nell looks up at Gran's face and Gran is seen answering. High angle: the moon passes the top edge without lingering.

beats.note: a short step back from the eyepiece (it ends facing right, toward Gran): the eyepiece clears her hair
Gran eases back a step as Nell steps back from the eyepiece, so they never overlap

beats.text: Gran, we're on the dot. Right now.
Right now, love. Both of us.

shots.note: screenplay 16.2. Wide, static. Nell sits on the grass; Gran sits down beside her (slowly); both look up while the sky goes from night to dawn. No words; the motif on music-box.

camera.note: tight enough that the hawthorn is wholly out of frame at the right (it was a half-tree sliver); the two of them larger as they sit

scenes.note: Part 12, screenplay scene 16 (dawn). They sit (Nell 2110, Gran 2215). Venus a steady white point (a skydot placed per shot): high on the left before sunrise (12.3, full strength), then up and to the right of the rising Sun, well clear of its glow and fading as the Sun clears the hills (12.4 a 0.6, 12.5 a 0.35); the Sun rises at the left in 12.4-12.5 (the shared sunrise piece).

shots.note: screenplay 16.3 (with the two lines the story review added: Gran asks Nell's own question from 0.4, Nell answers with Gran's lesson from 0.5). Full, low angle, the brightening sky. Venus low on the left. Nell turns to it and points, then back to Gran.

beats.text: Gran, that's not a star. That's Venus.

beats.name: point
beats.note: a second point while the first holds: the arm stays up through her line

beats.name: point
beats.note: and a third, to the end of the line

beats.name: point
beats.note: and a fourth, to the end of her line

beats.text: How can you tell?

beats.note: she turns round to Gran as Gran asks, and answers her face to face

beats.text: It shines so steady. Stars twinkle. Planets don't.
That's my clever girl.

shots.note: screenplay 16.4. Medium on both, static. The Sun's first edge comes up over the far hills at the left, warm light on their faces; one birdsong; the motif in full on tutti (the film's last cue, held under the end card).

camera.note: offset: the frame slides right so the tripod leg is out of frame and the rising Sun stands clear at about a fifth of the width (the eyepiece stays a small readable corner, top left); lower, so the captions sit on their knees and laps

beats.text: We turned back round to the Sun!
And that light left it eight minutes ago.

shots.note: screenplay 16.5. Wide, pull-out to establishing: the two small figures and the telescope on the crest in the morning light. The last four lines; the motif held under the end card.

beats.text: Thank you for the trip, Gran.
Thank you for the questions.
Same time tomorrow night?
Same time tomorrow night.
